title.narrative: Sustainable Labour Markets and Decent Work for Democracy

description.narrative: Workers worldwide face increasingly impossible choices—whether to feed or clothe their children—while governments and employers actively restrict their rights to demand fair wages and safe working conditions. The systematic erosion of trade union and labour rights threatens democracy and the rule of law. Union to Union’s global programme “Sustainable Labour Markets and Decent Work for Democracy” is developed in close collaboration with the global trade union movement, representing over 200 million members worldwide. The programme supports Sweden’s CSO strategy and will contribute to its two objectives. Its first objective is achieved by increasing the capacities of trade unions, and their leaders, members and activists, to be financially sustainable, democratic and accountable. The second objective is realised by strengthening collaboration among trade unions and bringing together the three parties of the labour market, the workers, the state and the employers, through social dialogue and collective bargaining. Ensuring the rightful existence of independent and accountable trade unions is critical, particularly in repressive environments, and for advancing a democratic civil society. Union to Union’s proposal aligns closely with Sida’s Operational Strategy, particularly in improving labour market conditions in countries affected by poverty and weak democratic structures. By leveraging social dialogue and internationally recognized labour standards, the programme bridges economic development with fair labour practices, ensuring that workers benefit from economic growth and climate policies. Union to Union’s programme is structured into thirty-two projects. With about 79 per cent of funds allocated to country-level projects, it prioritizes cost-effectiveness by utilizing existing trade union networks. Ultimately, this initiative strengthens local and national unions, equipping them to fight for decent work, democracy, and economic justice in an increasingly complex global labour market.
